content: Passionflower, scientifically known as Passiflora, is a genus comprising approximately 500 species of flowering plants within the family Passifloraceae. These plants are predominantly vines, although some species are shrubs, and a few are herbaceous. The fruit of the passionflower plant is commonly referred to as passion fruit. Biology The flowers of most decorative Passiflora species exhibit a unique structure that necessitates pollination by large bees. In the American tropics, wooden beams are often installed near passionfruit plantings to encourage nesting by carpenter bees, which are effective pollinators. The size and structure of the flowers vary significantly among different species. While some species are pollinated by hummingbirds and bumblebees, others rely on wasps or are capable of self-pollination. Certain species of Passiflora serve as food plants for the larvae of the moth Cibyra serta and various longwing butterflies (subfamily Heliconiinae), including notable species such as Heliconius melpomene, Heliconius sara, and Heliconius rosinia. The bracts of Passiflora foetida are covered with hairs that secrete a sticky fluid, which traps many insects. Research suggests that this may represent an adaptation similar to that of carnivorous plants. Origin The family Passifloraceae is distributed globally, except in Europe and Antarctica. Nine species are native to the United States, with passionflowers found as far north as Ohio, west to California, and south to the Florida Keys. They are also prevalent throughout most of South America, as well as in China, Southern Asia (17 species), New Guinea, Australia (four or more species), and New Zealand (one monotypic species). Africa hosts members of the Passifloraceae family, such as the primitive Adenia, but lacks Passiflora species. The purple-fruited Passiflora edulis and the yellow-fruited Passiflora edulis var. flavicarpa are widely cultivated in subtropical and tropical regions for their flavorful fruits. These two forms are considered distinct species, as they thrive in different climates, bloom at different times of the day, and exhibit varying reproductive behaviors. The purple-fruited species is self-fertile, while the yellow-fruited species is self-sterile and requires two clones for successful pollination. Cultivation During the Victorian era, passionflowers, which typically bloom for only one day, gained immense popularity. Numerous hybrids were developed using species such as Passiflora caerulea and Passiflora alata. Hundreds of hybrids have been named, and hybridization continues extensively for ornamental flowers, foliage, and fruit production. Many Passiflora species are cultivated outside their natural range for their striking flowers, with some becoming established in new environments. The passionfruit vine (Passiflora edulis), commercially known as maracujá, is extensively cultivated in the Caribbean, South Florida, and South Africa for its fruit, which is a popular source of juice. The maypop (Passiflora incarnata), a common species in the southeastern United States, is a subtropical representative of this predominantly tropical family. Unlike its tropical relatives, this species is hardy and can survive temperatures as low as -4°F (-20°C) before its roots die. Native as far north as Pennsylvania, it has been cultivated as far north as Boston. Its fruit is sweet, yellowish, and roughly the size of a chicken egg. The maypop is valued as a native plant with few pests and edible fruit. It also serves as a larval food source for various butterfly species and is important to local wildlife. Carpenter bees are key pollinators of maypops. The banana poka or curuba (Passiflora tarminiana), originally from Central Brazil, is an invasive weed in Hawaii, where feral pigs spread its fruits. It overgrows and smothers endemic vegetation, particularly along roadsides. While its fruits are edible, they are less sought after than maracujá. The Chilean passionflower (Passiflora pinnatistipula) grows in the Andes, from Venezuela to Chile, at altitudes between 2,500 and 3,800 meters. It is an endangered vine in the humid, woody Mediterranean forests of coastal central Chile. Most species produce elongated fruits ranging from 2 to 8 inches in length and 1 to 2 inches in diameter, depending on the species or cultivar. However, P. pinnatistipula has a round fruit, which is unusual for the Tacsonia group, characterized by species like P. tarminiana and P. mixta with their elongated tubes and brightly red to rose-colored petals. Medical and Entheogenic Uses The leaves and roots of Passiflora incarnata have a long history of use among Native Americans in North America. Similarly, Passiflora edulis and a few other species are used in Central and South America. The fresh or dried leaves are used to prepare an infusion or tea, which is employed to treat insomnia, hysteria, and epilepsy. It is also valued for its analgesic properties. Passiflora species contain beta-carboline harmala alkaloids, which are monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) with antidepressant properties. While the flowers contain only trace amounts of these chemicals, the leaves and roots of some species contain higher concentrations and have been used to enhance the effects of mind-altering drugs. Once dried, the leaves can also be smoked. Passionflower may also be effective in treating anxiety disorders, although further studies are required. Symbolism and Naming The name passion does not refer to romantic love but to the Passion of Christ on the cross. In the 15th and 16th centuries, Spanish Christian missionaries discovered this flower and interpreted its unique physical structures as symbols of the Crucifixion. For instance, the radial filaments, which can number over a hundred and vary from flower to flower, represent the Crown of Thorns. The ten petals and sepals symbolize the ten faithful apostles. The three stigmas represent the three nails, and the five anthers represent the five wounds of Christ. The flower has been given names related to this symbolism throughout Europe. In Spain, it is called Espina de Cristo (Christ's Thorn). In Germany, it was once known as Muttergottes-Schuzchen (Mother-of-God's Star). In Israel, it is referred to as clock-flower (שעונית). In Japan, it is known as clock-faced flower and has recently become a symbol for homosexual youths. In North America, it is also called the maypop, water lemon, and wild apricot, referencing its fruit. Native Americans in the Tennessee area called it ocoee, and the Ocoee River and valley are named after it.
